historical_timeline.summary: Born at Hvidtsten in Borge, Østfold.
Frostbitten fingers and a near-fatal night in a snow cave on a winter ski crossing of the Hardangervidda.
Scurvy aboard the Belgica in the Antarctic pack ice; recovery on fresh seal and penguin meat.
First voyage through the Northwest Passage in the Gjøa.
Fractured right shoulder and a polar bear attack on the Maud expedition.
Near-collapse from lamp fumes in the Maud's observatory, with months of palpitations on exertion.
A London heart specialist advised no more expeditions.
Back in Oslo after a lecture tour of Japan.
Left Uranienborg for the last time.
Lost with the Latham 47 over the Barents Sea during the search for the Italia's survivors.

claims.statement: Roald Engelbregt Gravning Amundsen was born on July 16, 1872, at the farm Hvidtsten in Borge, Østfold, Norway.

source_links.locator: born 16 July 1872 at Hvidtsten in Borge
authority record: born 1872-07-16, Borge

claims.statement: He wrote that as a young man he was near-sighted, a defect that had gradually improved but was not wholly corrected, and that he had refused to wear the glasses prescribed for him so that it would not keep him out of military training.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented myopia; anchors the modern eye examination.

source_links.locator: chapter I, military service

claims.statement: On a winter ski crossing of the Hardangervidda plateau in his early twenties he nearly died in a snow cave during a rest stop, and he wrote that he and his companion both got their fingers badly frostbitten while breaking into a nailed-up hut.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own documented frostbite of the fingers; anchors the modern late sequelae. The roster's 'frostbite' is supported for this event only.

source_links.locator: chapter I, the Hardangervidda crossing
near death in a snow cave

claims.statement: As first mate of the Belgian Antarctic expedition in the Belgica (1897 to 1899), he spent thirteen months in the pack ice. He wrote that every member of the ship's company was afflicted with scurvy and all but three were prostrated by it; once fresh seal and penguin meat was eaten, the men plainly improved within a week. The expedition's physician had encouraged the crew to eat seal and penguin.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents that he himself had scurvy by his own account, and the remedy. The physician is not named here.

source_links.locator: chapter II, ice-bound in the Antarctic
the physician encouraged eating seal and penguin
first mate on the Belgian expedition

claims.statement: A physician historian argues that the heart failure seen on the Belgica expedition, described at the time as 'polar anaemia', was almost certainly wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency, and that most sufferers were probably also deficient in vitamin C.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation about the expedition as a whole; not a claim about his own heart.

source_links.locator: abstract

claims.statement: He led the first voyage through the Northwest Passage in a single ship, the Gjøa (1903 to 1906), and on December 14, 1911, he and four companions were the first to reach the South Pole. In 1925 he led a flight by flying boat toward the North Pole from Ny-Ålesund, and in 1926 the flight of the airship Norge across the Arctic.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Career context; anchors his modern travel by air.

claims.statement: On the Maud expedition, in the autumn of 1918, he fell down the ship's runway onto his right shoulder; the fracture was set aboard by a crewman trained in first aid, and he kept to his bed for eight days. On November 8, 1918, a polar bear struck him on the back, leaving minor gashes. He wrote that he could not at first lift his right hand to use a pencil, worked the arm daily for months, and that a surgeon in Seattle who X-rayed it in 1921 found the shoulder in a condition that theoretically would make the arm unusable.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented complicated fracture of the upper arm with long rehabilitation.

source_links.locator: chapter on the northern ice pack
a complicated upper-arm fracture and a polar bear attack

claims.statement: About the New Year of 1918 to 1919, working in the small, unventilated observatory of the Maud with a kerosene vapour lamp, he became drowsy, felt his heart beating unnaturally, and nearly lost consciousness before he reached fresh air. He wrote that the violent palpitation lasted several days, that for months strenuous exercise set his heart pounding, and that in February he was exhausted by climbing a fifty-foot hill.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of the episode and its after-effects.

source_links.locator: chapter on the northern ice pack

claims.statement: He wrote that in February 1922 a heart specialist in London told him "No more expeditions!" and to avoid all strenuous exercise; nine months later he travelled about 800 miles on foot through the snow from Point Barrow to Nome, and five years later he wrote that he had had no unpleasant results from his exertions.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account; the specialist's findings are not recorded and no heart diagnosis is adopted.

source_links.locator: chapters on the Maud and on financial worries

claims.statement: The Norwegian encyclopedia describes the observatory episode as carbon monoxide poisoning.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; he himself was not sure whether the lamp used up the oxygen or gave off poisonous fumes.

source_links.locator: he was never sure exactly what happened

claims.statement: He bought the house Uranienborg at Svartskog, on the Bunnefjord near Oslo, in 1908 and lived there for twenty years. His study had an exercise spring installed in the floor for his strength training, and a pump brought salt water from the fjord for his morning bath.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented home and daily habits; anchors his exercise history.

source_links.locator: Uranienborg overview; the study; the bathroom

claims.statement: After his 1927 lecture tour of Japan he returned by the Trans-Siberian railway; letters place him in Oslo in August 1927 and again in May 1928.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Places him in Norway before and during the synthetic episode. The source is an auction catalogue description of his letters.

source_links.locator: letters of 18 August 1927 and 28 May 1928

claims.statement: The Norwegian encyclopedia writes that by the end of his career he felt tired, lonely and bitter; he was 55, with persistent money problems and no more poles to conquer. He had declared himself personally bankrupt.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented mood in an encyclopedia article; not a diagnosis. Anchors the modern depression screening only.

claims.statement: He left Uranienborg for the last time on June 16, 1928.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The synthetic episode ends before this date.

claims.statement: On the afternoon of June 18, 1928, he and five men flew from Tromsø toward Ny-Ålesund in a French Latham 47 flying boat to help search for the survivors of the crashed airship Italia. The aircraft disappeared, probably near Bjørnøya in the Barents Sea; all on board died, and only a float and a fuel tank were ever found.

source_links.locator: Tromsø, June 18; a float and a fuel tank
abstract
authority record: died about 1928-06-18

claims.statement: Historians reviewing the flight conclude that, in choosing a prototype aircraft that had not completed its flight tests and flying it unaccompanied over the Barents Sea despite warnings, he took a significant risk that led to his death and those of his crew.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. Retrospective interpretation; the modern risk discussion makes no prediction.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care and neurology for a 55-year-old polar explorer with cold-induced burning pain, numbness and color change in the fingers decades after frostbite: separating a late post-frostbite small-fiber neuropathy and cold-induced vasospasm from diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and nerve entrapment with blood tests and nerve conduction studies; cold protection and hand care; pharmacological management by NICE CG173, choosing capsaicin cream first because he wishes to avoid tablets and then duloxetine, a first-line drug less sedating than amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid for a man who flies and drives; monitoring of pain, adverse effects, mood, sleep, blood pressure and sodium; avoiding tramadol with duloxetine; preventive care at 55; and a risk discussion about an Arctic air search flight: cold-water immersion, re-injury of previously frostbitten fingers, a stiff old shoulder fracture, and carrying and not stopping duloxetine. Built on NICE CG173, the Wilderness Medical Society frostbite (1926) and hypothermia (1921) guidelines, and the USPSTF and CDC preventive recommendations.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Amundsen returns two weeks after his first visit, on the day of his neurology consultation with Dr. Abernathy-Dahl and nerve conduction studies this morning. The burning and numbness in his fingers come with every cold spell, on going outdoors, handling snow or cold metal, or washing in cold water, and last up to an hour after he comes indoors; the fingers turn white, then blue, then red as they rewarm. Between attacks the fingertips feel slightly numb. He has used liner gloves under mittens and hand warmers since the first visit, which helps. He has no weakness, no symptoms in his feet, and no wounds on the fingers. He does not want tablets that could make him drowsy.

assessment_plan.display: Post-frostbite cold-induced neuropathic pain and cold sensitivity of the fingers
assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting finger symptoms now have their explanation. Nerve conduction studies this morning are normal, with no carpal or cubital tunnel entrapment and no large-fiber polyneuropathy, and the digital sensory responses are low-normal. The intake blood tests exclude the common other causes: HbA1c 5.4%, fasting glucose 94 mg/dL, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL. With reduced pinprick and cold sensation at the fingertips, cold allodynia, and cold-induced color change, Dr. Abernathy-Dahl diagnoses a small-fiber neuropathy with vasospasm as a late sequela of his frostbite. Average pain 6 of 10 at intake. He wishes to avoid oral treatment, so capsaicin cream is the first choice under NICE CG173
plan: Capsaicin 0.075% cream four times a day to the painful fingers
Continue liner and heated gloves and hand warmers; warm the hands before fine work
Review in four weeks; oral duloxetine if the cream is not enough

hpi.narrative: Mr. Amundsen returns four weeks after starting capsaicin cream. It stung for the first week and he has used it about three times a day. The burning is a little less, but the cold attacks still come most days in the late winter weather, and his average pain over the past week is 5 of 10. He still wakes some nights. He is willing now to try a tablet if it will not make him drowsy, because he drives and expects to fly again. He drinks rarely and takes no other medicines.

referral.question: Cold-induced burning pain, numbness and color change in the fingers of both hands for many winters, worse this winter, in a 55-year-old polar explorer with frostbite of the fingers in early adulthood. Please confirm or exclude a late post-frostbite neuropathy, nerve entrapment, or another polyneuropathy, and advise on treatment that will not make him drowsy, as he drives and flies
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, with nerve conduction studies
referral.pertinent_history: Burning pain and numbness in the index to little fingers of both hands, brought on by cold and lasting up to an hour after rewarming, with the fingers turning white, then blue, then red; slight fingertip numbness between attacks; average pain 6 of 10 over the past week. No weakness, no foot symptoms, no ulcers. Frostbite of the fingers of both hands on a winter ski crossing in his early twenties. Old fracture of the right upper arm, treated without surgery, with limited overhead reach. Never smoked; alcohol rare. No regular medicines. Examination today: cool fingertips with slightly delayed capillary refill, reduced pinprick at the fingertips, normal strength and reflexes, normal radial and ulnar pulses. Sodium 141 and potassium 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 93), fasting glucose 94 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.4%, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL. PHQ-9 5. He fears he can no longer work in the Arctic, and he does not want a medicine that causes drowsiness
questions: Is this a late neuropathy from his old frostbite, or is there an entrapment or another cause?
Are nerve conduction studies or other tests needed?
What treatment do you recommend, given that he wishes to avoid drowsiness and, at first, tablets?
How should the cold-induced color change be managed?
How can he protect his fingers if he works in the cold again?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Amundsen, a 55-year-old polar explorer, is seen at the request of Dr. Solheim-Achebe for burning pain and numbness in the fingers of both hands brought on by cold. The attacks have come every winter for many years and have been worse this winter, lasting up to an hour after he comes indoors, with the fingers turning white, then blue, then red. Between attacks the fingertips are slightly numb. There is no weakness, clumsiness apart from the cold, foot symptoms, neck pain, or night-time tingling that wakes him in warm weather. He had frostbite of the fingers of both hands in his early twenties. He has never smoked, drinks rarely, and takes no regular medicines. He drives, flies as a passenger and navigator, and would rather avoid tablets, and certainly any that make him drowsy
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Solheim-Achebe's intake note and blood tests: HbA1c 5.4%, fasting glucose 94 mg/dL, vitamin B12 512 pg/mL, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, ALT 24 U/L, hemoglobin 14.9 g/dL. Nerve conduction studies today: median, ulnar and radial sensory and motor conduction normal in both arms, with normal distal latencies and no slowing across the elbow; median-ulnar palmar comparison normal; digital sensory responses low-normal and symmetric

exam.finding: Well; blood pressure 126/78, pulse 60
Fingertips cool with slightly delayed capillary refill; no ulcers, pitting or scars; normal radial and ulnar pulses
Reduced pinprick and cold sensation at the tips of the index to little fingers of both hands; cold allodynia on a cold tuning fork; vibration and joint position normal
Normal bulk and strength in both hands, including thumb abduction and finger abduction; reflexes normal and symmetric
Tinel sign at wrist and elbow and Phalen test negative on both sides

assessment.display: Post-frostbite small-fiber neuropathy and cold-induced vasospasm of the fingers
assessment.assessment: The history of frostbite, the fingertip distribution, the loss of pinprick and cold sensation with cold allodynia, the normal large-fiber function, and the cold-induced color change fit a late small-fiber neuropathy with vasospasm after frostbite, which is recognized as a long-term consequence. Normal nerve conduction studies exclude carpal and cubital tunnel syndromes and a large-fiber polyneuropathy, and the blood tests exclude diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and kidney disease. No further tests are needed. Skin biopsy for small-fiber density would not change management

He wishes to avoid oral treatment, and the pain is localized to the fingers, so capsaicin cream is reasonable first under NICE CG173. If it is not enough, duloxetine is the best of the first-line oral drugs for him, because amitriptyline, gabapentin and pregabalin are more likely to cause drowsiness; tramadol should be avoided, both because it is not for long-term use and because it interacts with duloxetine

Secondary to the old cold injury. No ulcers or signs of critical ischemia. Cold protection is the main treatment; a calcium-channel blocker would be considered only if attacks remained frequent and severe despite it

recommendations: Capsaicin 0.075% cream to the painful fingers four times a day, washing the hands after use; it may sting for the first week

If pain remains troublesome after four weeks, duloxetine 30 mg daily for a week, then 60 mg daily, with review of pain, adverse effects, mood, sleep and blood pressure, a sodium and liver enzyme check in the first weeks, no tramadol, and no abrupt stopping
Cold protection: liner gloves under mittens, heated gloves and hand warmers, warming the hands before fine work, no cold-water hand washing, and checking the skin for injury
No calcium-channel blocker for now; reconsider if attacks of vasospasm stay frequent and severe
Previously frostbitten fingers are more vulnerable to cold injury: in cold work, extra insulation, frequent checks, and early rewarming
No further tests; neurology review only if weakness, spreading sensory loss, or ulceration develops
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Solheim-Achebe, who saw him the same day. The results and options were explained to Mr. Amundsen, who chose to start with the cream and agreed with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Neurology review on request; primary care review in four weeks
